meters.label: Requests per second sent to dead p2

frames.narration: Orders has payment's addresses written into its config: p1 and p2. Round-robin spreads its 30 requests per second, 15 to each. At t=60 s the autoscaler starts p3 on a new IP address, and orders never sends it a single request.
At t=155 s p2 crashes. The config still lists it, so half of all calls, 15 per second, go to a dead address: 900 failures a minute until someone edits the file and restarts orders.

Fix: a registry. Each instance registers itself on start-up with its name, address and port. The entry is a lease with a 30 s time to live, renewed by a heartbeat every 10 s, so two lost heartbeats are tolerated.

Orders opens a watch on 'payment'. It gets the list once, keeps it in memory, and each change is pushed within about 1 s. It picks instances itself (client-side discovery): 30 requests per second over 3 instances is 10 each, with no lookup per request.

p2 crashes at t=155 s. Its last heartbeat was at t=150 s, so its lease runs out at 150 + 30 = 180 s. The registry removes p2 and pushes the change, and orders stops calling it at 181 s: 26 s x 10 requests = 260 failed calls, or none if each failure is retried once on another instance.

The same registry can answer DNS: payment.service.consul returns p1, p2 and p3 with a 30 s TTL. If orders resolved the name at t=179 s, it keeps p2 until 209 s, 54 s after the crash: 540 failed calls instead of 260. Worst case is lease TTL plus DNS TTL.

Some clients ignore the TTL: a runtime that caches lookups for the life of the process, or a pooled keep-alive connection, keeps using p2's address long after DNS dropped it. That caller is back to the config-file problem.

Now 2 of the registry's 3 Raft servers fail. Without a majority it accepts no registrations or removals. Orders keeps serving from its cached list, which goes slowly stale. A caller that asked the registry on every request would fail every call.
